title: Everybody needs a personal AI policy. Just ask Hank Green.
excerpt: How to use AI for research and creative work without outsourcing too much of your thinking.
content_html:
Everyone is wrong about Hank Green.

In case you missed the controversy: The veteran YouTube star, writer, and science comms entrepreneur was recently “canceled” after he acknowledged using AI for research.

“I have been relying too heavily on AI as a research aid,” he wrote in a statement on Reddit. “It can be very useful for this task, giving me access to a lot of papers I didn’t know existed really fast, but I think that has been to the detriment of my work because it has not given me the freedom to find all of my own ways into and around a topic.” Although Green wrote that the words in his videos are his own, his reliance on AI as a research aid still gave the finished work an ineffable “AI feel.” And his relationship with AI, he wrote, had become “not healthy for me or good for the world.”

Some of Green’s followers, known by the cheerfully dorky moniker “Nerdfighters,” turned on him for daring to use AI in any capacity. Just as quickly, that backlash produced its own backlash, aghast not at Green’s use of AI but at his prostration before an anti-AI mob — “self-canceling,” as some put it, over a legitimate use of the technology.

I think both of these camps are misguided and have flattened a complex issue into a set of binary extremes. And it surprised me that, despite robust societal debate on AI’s impacts on our ability to think, write, and produce original ideas, the debacle hasn’t prompted more thoughtful conversation about the limits of AI in creative work.

I felt this because I recognized myself in Green’s statement: the feeling that even using AI for research can start to take over your creative process, that it can become hard to know where your own brain ends and where AI begins, and that the technology can simply push you to work too fast. I don’t use AI to generate writing and would not do so — but its use need not rise to that level to raise profound questions about how much of our work to automate, and what happens to our ability to think for ourselves when we do.

In a follow-up video published late last week, Green laid out a new AI policy for his work. He wrote:

1. No portion of any script will be written, edited, or outlined by an LLM.

2. The thesis of a video will always originate with a human.

3. No image or music in a video will be generated by AI. If something is accidentally included, best efforts will be made to remove it.

4. LLM outputs are not trusted as a source.

These are all good ideas for any creator trying to avoid AI creep in their craft. But still, they raise a bigger, harder-to-answer question: The very structure of generative AI makes it hard to use without offloading human thought and judgment, which can lead to a widely discussed phenomenon known as “cognitive surrender.” And it pushes us toward uses — like synthesizing research, brainstorming, generating ideas and angles — that short-circuit the original thinking and discovery that we ought to be doing ourselves. What, then, can we even responsibly use AI for? How can we set guardrails that allow us to avail ourselves of its usefulness, without melting our brains in the process?

The most tempting uses of AI are precisely those best avoided

Remember late 2022, when ChatGPT first came out and everyone mocked its crappy research skills and propensity to hallucinate in every other sentence? I am so wistful for those days.

Many people who abstain from AI may not know it, but in the time since, and especially in recent months, large language models have gotten way smarter (especially the paid premium versions). It’s become unnervingly good at summarizing niche, complex research areas and debates, and producing ideas, often without being asked, for further research or writing on the same subject.

Whenever I have a research question these days (which is pretty much any time I’m working on a story), I’m more likely to fire up an LLM than a traditional search engine. If I ask, “Why are old-growth trees still being logged in North America?” it produces a synthesis of research, news, opinion, and whatever else its training absorbed on the subject: “We’re using an essentially nonrenewable ecological asset to smooth a temporary transition to a renewable timber resource,” it says. Probe it further, and it’ll suggest arguments for you: “Instead of conservationists having to prove that every old forest deserves protection, logging companies should have to demonstrate that cutting a centuries-old stand serves a need that cannot reasonably be met with second-growth or engineered wood.”

LLMs are designed to make cognitive work effortless, but that feels so icky because for it to be worthwhile at all, it has to be effortful.

These aren’t particularly smart or creative ideas — they’re perfectly replacement-level, which makes them plausible substitutes for the thoughts of most people. The AI can supply pat answers to every conceivable question and follow-up you might have while working on a project, relieving you of the need to mentally engage with the shape of a problem. Contrast that with Googling in the pre-AI overview days, which, while certainly not without its problems, at least used to send you to a list of sources that you then had to read and make sense of on your own.

Most of us who’ve engaged with LLMs know what this feels like. They make it easy for users to skate on the surface of a subject and feign understanding or insight, and in the process they can become involved in interpretive decisions that should be our own. In my experience, even more narrowly designed generative AI models don’t escape these problems. Google’s Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM), for example, allows you to upload all of your sources for a project — books, reports, papers, audio and video recordings — and ask it questions based on what they contain, rather than searching the entire internet. It’s less prone to generating outright slop than general-purpose AIs. I use it for most stories I write — it’s an incredibly useful, time-saving tool. But it also enables me to engage with sources in a perfunctory, contextless manner: The AI can surface precisely the bit I need rather than forcing me to form the deeper connections that come from reading a text as a whole.

The best creative work (including not just art and writing, but also technological and medical breakthroughs) probably comes from having a wide range of background associations, and being able to combine them in unexpected ways. The French mathematician Henri Poincaré put this beautifully in his essay “Mathematical Creation,” where he wrote that it’s the tedious, sustained conscious effort that ultimately leads to flashes of insight.

I think this is what Green meant when he wrote that AI can prevent him from finding his “own ways into and around a topic.” LLMs are designed to make cognitive work effortless, but that feels so icky because for it to be worthwhile at all, it has to be effortful. This argument has already been made about AI-generated writing: Letting an LLM write for you defeats the point, because writing is thinking. But it can also be true, as Green’s example has shown, of using AI for the research that feeds the creative process.

If you use AI, consider creating a personal AI policy

Perhaps all these concerns are overblown — humans are hardly less prone to lazy and logically unsound thinking than AI. That’s absolutely true, but the point of doing our own thinking isn’t that we’re inherently good at it. To the contrary, it’s that we can only get better at reasoning by practicing it.

I don’t want to suggest that using AI for research is illegitimate. It’s too useful a tool to take off the table entirely, and we can’t put that genie back in the bottle. It can be extremely helpful with identifying the best sources that you wouldn’t find otherwise, but those very abilities can make it double-edged, foreclosing a slower, more open-ended exploration process. But AI’s greatest strength — its endless variety and flexibility — can be used to steer it away from the most tempting uses, especially those that ultimately harm us.

How to practice good AI hygiene

  • Don’t use AI to form your thesis or core arguments.
  • Use AI to find, not replace, sources, and avoid depending on AI-generated syntheses of sources. Read through source material yourself.
  • Keep creative borrowing of AI-generated language microscopic, not much different from how you’d use a thesaurus.
  • Watch out for compulsive chatbot use.

There are very obvious things that any LLM user should do to that end, like never assuming that a claim from an AI is accurate and always reading original sources. Beyond that, the necessary guardrails depend on your own use patterns, but above all, I think it’s helpful to avoid training ourselves to expect immediate answers to difficult questions.

One of my colleagues refrains from using it to brainstorm ideas entirely, instead using it to provide sources for narrow factual questions and to aid in the fact-checking process (emphasis on “aid”) after a story is written. To generalize from this, I think it’s a good idea to resist having AI do much synthetic work on a subject before you have drafted your project yourself. The less you do that, the less you will, to paraphrase Green’s recent video, see every problem as an “LLM-shaped problem,” and the less you’ll feel like you’re in the singularity where your brain is merging with AI.

One way that I like to use AI is as an enhanced thesaurus, to find the precise word or short phrase to express what I want to say in a sentence. When done right, I don’t find this harmful any more than using a traditional thesaurus; I find that it can enrich my working lexicon. But it must be used carefully and surgically, by setting a clear limit on the length of a phrase used from AI — like two or three words max — and avoiding sharing much of your writing with the tool at all, lest it start recommending extensive rewrites.

When interrogating the contents of specific sources or a body of work, or stress testing your own arguments, AI would be better for our intellectual development if it took a Socratic approach — pushing you to discover an answer rather than simply giving you one. It might say, for example, “there might be some relevant caveats to your idea on pp. 42-43 of the source.” LLMs can be directed to behave this way in their custom instructions. It also helps to simply touch grass — find the sources you need, and rather than interviewing the AI about what they say, just close the chatbot and read them from start to finish.

Configuring AI in a way that’s healthier for our brains would also make it less addictive — when you find yourself getting sucked into a long back-and-forth with an AI, that’s often a sign that something has gone amiss. Green evidently struggled to set that boundary, referencing the unhealthy “level of dopamine I’ve been getting from interacting with LLMs.” AI labs have very strong commercial incentives to want us to be addicted to their products, and unless they build different constraints into models themselves, it’s hard to expect the average person, who has far less autonomy over the terms of her work than Green does, to change these conditions on her own.

Although researchers at some AI labs are thinking about the societal risks of cognitive atrophy, it’s another matter to expect these companies, which compete on ease of use, to introduce friction into their models. We shouldn’t count on that happening soon — but we’re far from powerless against AI’s impacts. We can set our own personal AI use policies, and we can enforce social norms against AI-induced brain rot. Like, at bare minimum: Don’t send me your AI-generated writing. It’s rude!

blocks.html_en: These are all good ideas for any creator trying to avoid AI creep in their craft. But still, they raise a bigger, harder-to-answer question: The very structure of generative AI makes it hard to use without offloading human thought and judgment, which can lead to a widely discussed phenomenon known as “cognitive surrender.” And it pushes us toward uses — like synthesizing research, brainstorming, generating ideas and angles — that short-circuit the original thinking and discovery that we ought to be doing ourselves. What, then, can we even responsibly use AI for? How can we set guardrails that allow us to avail ourselves of its usefulness, without melting our brains in the process?

sentences.en: These are all good ideas for any creator trying to avoid AI creep in their craft.
sentences.zh: 对于任何试图避免人工智能在其作品中蔓延的创作者来说，这些都是好主意。

sentences.en: But still, they raise a bigger, harder-to-answer question: The very structure of generative AI makes it hard to use without offloading human thought and judgment, which can lead to a widely discussed phenomenon known as “cognitive surrender.”
sentences.zh: 但他们仍然提出了一个更大、更难回答的问题：生成式人工智能的结构本身就使得它很难在不减轻人类思维和判断力的情况下使用，这可能导致一种被广泛讨论的现象，即“认知投降”。

sentences.en: And it pushes us toward uses — like synthesizing research, brainstorming, generating ideas and angles — that short-circuit the original thinking and discovery that we ought to be doing ourselves.
sentences.zh: 它推动我们走向各种用途——比如综合研究、集思广益、产生想法和角度——从而缩短了我们应该自己做的原始思考和发现。

sentences.en: What, then, can we even responsibly use AI for?
sentences.zh: 那么，我们可以负责任地使用人工智能做什么呢？

sentences.en: How can we set guardrails that allow us to avail ourselves of its usefulness, without melting our brains in the process?
sentences.zh: 我们怎样才能设置护栏，让我们能够利用它的用处，同时又不会在这个过程中融化我们的大脑呢？

blocks.html_en: The most tempting uses of AI are precisely those best avoided

sentences.en: The most tempting uses of AI are precisely those best avoided
sentences.zh: 人工智能最诱人的用途恰恰是最好避免的用途

blocks.html_en: Remember late 2022, when ChatGPT first came out and everyone mocked its crappy research skills and propensity to hallucinate in every other sentence? I am so wistful for those days.

sentences.en: Remember late 2022, when ChatGPT first came out and everyone mocked its crappy research skills and propensity to hallucinate in every other sentence?
sentences.zh: 还记得 2022 年末，当 ChatGPT 首次问世时，每个人都嘲笑它蹩脚的研究能力和每一句话都会产生幻觉的倾向吗？

sentences.en: I am so wistful for those days.
sentences.zh: 我非常怀念那些日子。

blocks.html_en: Many people who abstain from AI may not know it, but in the time since, and especially in recent months, large language models have gotten way smarter (especially the paid premium versions). It’s become unnervingly good at summarizing niche, complex research areas and debates, and producing ideas, often without being asked, for further research or writing on the same subject.

sentences.en: Many people who abstain from AI may not know it, but in the time since, and especially in recent months, large language models have gotten way smarter (especially the paid premium versions).
sentences.zh: 许多放弃人工智能的人可能不知道，但从那时起，特别是最近几个月，大型语言模型已经变得更加智能（尤其是付费高级版本）。

sentences.en: It’s become unnervingly good at summarizing niche, complex research areas and debates, and producing ideas, often without being asked, for further research or writing on the same subject.
sentences.zh: 它非常擅长总结利基、复杂的研究领域和辩论，并经常在没有被要求的情况下提出想法，以进行同一主题的进一步研究或写作。

blocks.html_en: Whenever I have a research question these days (which is pretty much any time I’m working on a story), I’m more likely to fire up an LLM than a traditional search engine. If I ask, “Why are old-growth trees still being logged in North America?” it produces a synthesis of research, news, opinion, and whatever else its training absorbed on the subject: “We’re using an essentially nonrenewable ecological asset to smooth a temporary transition to a renewable timber resource,” it says. Probe it further, and it’ll suggest arguments for you: “Instead of conservationists having to prove that every old forest deserves protection, logging companies should have to demonstrate that cutting a centuries-old stand serves a need that cannot reasonably be met with second-growth or engineered wood.”

sentences.zh: 法学硕士旨在让认知工作变得毫不费力，但这感觉很恶心，因为它必须付出努力才有价值。

blocks.html_en: These aren’t particularly smart or creative ideas — they’re perfectly replacement-level, which makes them plausible substitutes for the thoughts of most people. The AI can supply pat answers to every conceivable question and follow-up you might have while working on a project, relieving you of the need to mentally engage with the shape of a problem. Contrast that with Googling in the pre-AI overview days, which, while certainly not without its problems, at least used to send you to a list of sources that you then had to read and make sense of on your own.

sentences.zh: 人工智能可以为您在项目工作中可能遇到的每个可以想到的问题和后续行动提供简单的答案，使您无需在精神上思考问题的形状。

sentences.en: Contrast that with Googling in the pre-AI overview days, which, while certainly not without its problems, at least used to send you to a list of sources that you then had to read and make sense of on your own.
sentences.zh: 与人工智能概述时代之前的谷歌搜索相比，谷歌搜索虽然肯定存在问题，但至少用于将您发送到一系列来源，然后您必须自己阅读并理解这些来源。

blocks.html_en: Most of us who’ve engaged with LLMs know what this feels like. They make it easy for users to skate on the surface of a subject and feign understanding or insight, and in the process they can become involved in interpretive decisions that should be our own. In my experience, even more narrowly designed generative AI models don’t escape these problems. Google’s Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM), for example, allows you to upload all of your sources for a project — books, reports, papers, audio and video recordings — and ask it questions based on what they contain, rather than searching the entire internet. It’s less prone to generating outright slop than general-purpose AIs. I use it for most stories I write — it’s an incredibly useful, time-saving tool. But it also enables me to engage with sources in a perfunctory, contextless manner: The AI can surface precisely the bit I need rather than forcing me to form the deeper connections that come from reading a text as a whole.

sentences.en: Most of us who’ve engaged with LLMs know what this feels like.
sentences.zh: 我们大多数接触过法学硕士的人都知道这是什么感觉。

sentences.zh: 但它也使我能够以一种敷衍的、无上下文的方式与来源互动：人工智能可以准确地呈现我需要的部分，而不是强迫我通过阅读整个文本来形成更深层次的联系。

blocks.html_en: The best creative work (including not just art and writing, but also technological and medical breakthroughs) probably comes from having a wide range of background associations, and being able to combine them in unexpected ways. The French mathematician Henri Poincaré put this beautifully in his essay “Mathematical Creation,” where he wrote that it’s the tedious, sustained conscious effort that ultimately leads to flashes of insight.

sentences.en: The best creative work (including not just art and writing, but also technological and medical breakthroughs) probably comes from having a wide range of background associations, and being able to combine them in unexpected ways.
sentences.zh: 最好的创意作品（不仅包括艺术和写作，还包括技术和医学突破）可能来自于拥有广泛的背景关联，并能够以意想不到的方式将它们结合起来。

sentences.en: The French mathematician Henri Poincaré put this beautifully in his essay “Mathematical Creation,” where he wrote that it’s the tedious, sustained conscious effort that ultimately leads to flashes of insight.
sentences.zh: 法国数学家亨利·庞加莱（Henri Poincaré）在他的文章《数学创造》中完美地表达了这一点，他在文中写道，繁琐、持续的有意识的努力最终会带来洞察力的闪现。

blocks.html_en: I think this is what Green meant when he wrote that AI can prevent him from finding his “own ways into and around a topic.” LLMs are designed to make cognitive work effortless, but that feels so icky because for it to be worthwhile at all, it has to be effortful. This argument has already been made about AI-generated writing: Letting an LLM write for you defeats the point, because writing is thinking. But it can also be true, as Green’s example has shown, of using AI for the research that feeds the creative process.

sentences.en: I think this is what Green meant when he wrote that AI can prevent him from finding his “own ways into and around a topic.”
sentences.zh: 我认为这就是格林在写道人工智能可以阻止他找到“自己进入和围绕某个主题的方式”时的意思。

sentences.en: LLMs are designed to make cognitive work effortless, but that feels so icky because for it to be worthwhile at all, it has to be effortful.
sentences.zh: 法学硕士旨在让认知工作变得毫不费力，但这感觉很恶心，因为它必须付出努力才有价值。

sentences.zh: 但正如格林的例子所表明的那样，使用人工智能进行支持创造性过程的研究也可能是正确的。

blocks.html_en: If you use AI, consider creating a personal AI policy

sentences.en: If you use AI, consider creating a personal AI policy
sentences.zh: 如果您使用人工智能，请考虑制定个人人工智能政策

blocks.html_en: Perhaps all these concerns are overblown — humans are hardly less prone to lazy and logically unsound thinking than AI. That’s absolutely true, but the point of doing our own thinking isn’t that we’re inherently good at it. To the contrary, it’s that we can only get better at reasoning by practicing it.

sentences.en: Perhaps all these concerns are overblown — humans are hardly less prone to lazy and logically unsound thinking than AI.
sentences.zh: 也许所有这些担忧都被夸大了——人类比人工智能更容易出现懒惰和逻辑不健全的思维。

sentences.en: That’s absolutely true, but the point of doing our own thinking isn’t that we’re inherently good at it.
sentences.zh: 这是绝对正确的，但我们自己思考的意义并不在于我们天生就擅长它。

sentences.en: To the contrary, it’s that we can only get better at reasoning by practicing it.
sentences.zh: 相反，我们只有通过练习才能提高推理能力。

blocks.html_en: I don’t want to suggest that using AI for research is illegitimate. It’s too useful a tool to take off the table entirely, and we can’t put that genie back in the bottle. It can be extremely helpful with identifying the best sources that you wouldn’t find otherwise, but those very abilities can make it double-edged, foreclosing a slower, more open-ended exploration process. But AI’s greatest strength — its endless variety and flexibility — can be used to steer it away from the most tempting uses, especially those that ultimately harm us.

sentences.en: I don’t want to suggest that using AI for research is illegitimate.
sentences.zh: 我不想说使用人工智能进行研究是非法的。

sentences.en: It’s too useful a tool to take off the table entirely, and we can’t put that genie back in the bottle.
sentences.zh: 这是一个非常有用的工具，无法完全从桌子上取下来，而且我们不能把那个精灵放回瓶子里。

sentences.en: It can be extremely helpful with identifying the best sources that you wouldn’t find otherwise, but those very abilities can make it double-edged, foreclosing a slower, more open-ended exploration process.
sentences.zh: 它对于识别你无法找到的最佳来源非常有帮助，但正是这些能力使其成为一把双刃剑，阻碍了更慢、更开放的探索过程。

sentences.en: But AI’s greatest strength — its endless variety and flexibility — can be used to steer it away from the most tempting uses, especially those that ultimately harm us.
sentences.zh: 但人工智能最大的优势——其无尽的多样性和灵活性——可以用来引导它远离最具诱惑力的用途，尤其是那些最终伤害我们的用途。

blocks.html_en: How to practice good AI hygiene

sentences.en: How to practice good AI hygiene
sentences.zh: 如何保持良好的人工智能卫生习惯

blocks.html_en: • Don’t use AI to form your thesis or core arguments.

sentences.en: Don’t use AI to form your thesis or core arguments.
sentences.zh: 不要使用人工智能来形成你的论文或核心论点。

blocks.html_en: • Use AI to find, not replace, sources, and avoid depending on AI-generated syntheses of sources. Read through source material yourself.

sentences.en: Use AI to find, not replace, sources, and avoid depending on AI-generated syntheses of sources.
sentences.zh: 使用人工智能来查找而不是替换来源，并避免依赖人工智能生成的来源合成。

sentences.en: Read through source material yourself.
sentences.zh: 自己通读源材料。

blocks.html_en: • Keep creative borrowing of AI-generated language microscopic, not much different from how you’d use a thesaurus.

sentences.en: Keep creative borrowing of AI-generated language microscopic, not much different from how you’d use a thesaurus.
sentences.zh: 保持人工智能生成语言的创造性借用微观化，与使用同义词库的方式没有太大区别。

blocks.html_en: • Watch out for compulsive chatbot use.

sentences.en: Watch out for compulsive chatbot use.
sentences.zh: 留意强制使用聊天机器人。

blocks.html_en: There are very obvious things that any LLM user should do to that end, like never assuming that a claim from an AI is accurate and always reading original sources. Beyond that, the necessary guardrails depend on your own use patterns, but above all, I think it’s helpful to avoid training ourselves to expect immediate answers to difficult questions.

sentences.en: There are very obvious things that any LLM user should do to that end, like never assuming that a claim from an AI is accurate and always reading original sources.
sentences.zh: 为此，任何法学硕士用户都应该做一些非常明显的事情，比如永远不要假设人工智能的主张是准确的，并且总是阅读原始资料。

sentences.en: Beyond that, the necessary guardrails depend on your own use patterns, but above all, I think it’s helpful to avoid training ourselves to expect immediate answers to difficult questions.
sentences.zh: 除此之外，必要的护栏取决于您自己的使用模式，但最重要的是，我认为避免训练自己期待难题的立即答案是有帮助的。

blocks.html_en: One of my colleagues refrains from using it to brainstorm ideas entirely, instead using it to provide sources for narrow factual questions and to aid in the fact-checking process (emphasis on “aid”) after a story is written. To generalize from this, I think it’s a good idea to resist having AI do much synthetic work on a subject before you have drafted your project yourself. The less you do that, the less you will, to paraphrase Green’s recent video, see every problem as an “LLM-shaped problem,” and the less you’ll feel like you’re in the singularity where your brain is merging with AI.

sentences.en: One of my colleagues refrains from using it to brainstorm ideas entirely, instead using it to provide sources for narrow factual questions and to aid in the fact-checking process (emphasis on “aid”) after a story is written.
sentences.zh: 我的一位同事不会完全用它来集思广益，而是用它来为狭隘的事实问题提供来源，并在故事写完后帮助进行事实核查过程（强调“帮助”）。

sentences.en: To generalize from this, I think it’s a good idea to resist having AI do much synthetic work on a subject before you have drafted your project yourself.
sentences.zh: 综上所述，我认为在你自己起草项目之前，最好不要让人工智能对某个主题进行大量综合工作。

sentences.en: The less you do that, the less you will, to paraphrase Green’s recent video, see every problem as an “LLM-shaped problem,” and the less you’ll feel like you’re in the singularity where your brain is merging with AI.
sentences.zh: 你做的越少，你就越不会将每个问题视为“LLM 型问题”，用格林最近的视频的话来说，你就越不会感觉自己处于大脑与人工智能融合的奇点中。

blocks.html_en: One way that I like to use AI is as an enhanced thesaurus, to find the precise word or short phrase to express what I want to say in a sentence. When done right, I don’t find this harmful any more than using a traditional thesaurus; I find that it can enrich my working lexicon. But it must be used carefully and surgically, by setting a clear limit on the length of a phrase used from AI — like two or three words max — and avoiding sharing much of your writing with the tool at all, lest it start recommending extensive rewrites.

sentences.en: One way that I like to use AI is as an enhanced thesaurus, to find the precise word or short phrase to express what I want to say in a sentence.
sentences.zh: 我喜欢使用人工智能的一种方式是作为增强的同义词库，找到精确的单词或短语来表达我想说的句子。

blocks.html_en: When interrogating the contents of specific sources or a body of work, or stress testing your own arguments, AI would be better for our intellectual development if it took a Socratic approach — pushing you to discover an answer rather than simply giving you one. It might say, for example, “there might be some relevant caveats to your idea on pp. 42-43 of the source.” LLMs can be directed to behave this way in their custom instructions. It also helps to simply touch grass — find the sources you need, and rather than interviewing the AI about what they say, just close the chatbot and read them from start to finish.

blocks.html_en: Configuring AI in a way that’s healthier for our brains would also make it less addictive — when you find yourself getting sucked into a long back-and-forth with an AI, that’s often a sign that something has gone amiss. Green evidently struggled to set that boundary, referencing the unhealthy “level of dopamine I’ve been getting from interacting with LLMs.” AI labs have very strong commercial incentives to want us to be addicted to their products, and unless they build different constraints into models themselves, it’s hard to expect the average person, who has far less autonomy over the terms of her work than Green does, to change these conditions on her own.

blocks.html_en: Although researchers at some AI labs are thinking about the societal risks of cognitive atrophy, it’s another matter to expect these companies, which compete on ease of use, to introduce friction into their models. We shouldn’t count on that happening soon — but we’re far from powerless against AI’s impacts. We can set our own personal AI use policies, and we can enforce social norms against AI-induced brain rot. Like, at bare minimum: Don’t send me your AI-generated writing. It’s rude!

content_html_zh:
每个人对汉克·格林的看法都是错误的。

如果你错过了这场争议：这位资深的 YouTube 明星、作家和科学传播企业家最近在承认使用人工智能进行研究后被“取消”。

“我一直过于依赖人工智能作为研究辅助手段，”他在 Reddit 上的一份声明中写道。 “它对于这项任务非常有用，让我能够快速获得很多我不知道的论文，但我认为这对我的工作不利，因为它没有让我自由地找到自己进入和围绕某个主题的所有方式。” 尽管格林写道，视频中的文字是他自己的，但他对人工智能作为研究辅助的依赖仍然给完成的作品带来了一种不可言喻的“人工智能感觉”。 他写道，他与人工智能的关系已经变得“对我来说不健康，对世界也不有利”。

格林的一些追随者（被称为“书呆子战士”）的一些追随者因他敢于以任何方式使用人工智能而对他发起攻击。 同样，这种强烈反对很快又引发了强烈反对，令人震惊的不是格林对人工智能的使用，而是他在反人工智能暴民面前的屈服——用一些人的话来说，这是对技术合法使用的“自我取消”。

未来完美

探索世界面临的重大、复杂的问题以及解决这些问题的最有效方法。 每周发送两次。

电子邮件（必填）

我认为这两个阵营都被误导了，并将一个复杂的问题简化为一组二元极端。 令我惊讶的是，尽管社会上就人工智能对我们思考、写作和产生原创想法的能力的影响展开了激烈的争论，但这场灾难并没有引发人们对人工智能在创造性工作中的局限性进行更深入的讨论。

我之所以有这种感觉，是因为我在格林的陈述中认识到了自己：这种感觉，即使使用人工智能进行研究也可能开始接管你的创作过程，你可能很难知道你自己的大脑在哪里结束，人工智能在哪里开始，而且这项技术只会让你工作得太快。 我不会使用人工智能来生成写作，也不会这样做——但它的使用不必上升到这样的水平，从而引发一些深刻的问题：我们有多少工作需要自动化，以及当我们这样做时，我们的独立思考能力会发生什么变化。

在上周晚些时候发布的后续视频中，格林为其工作制定了新的人工智能政策。 他写道：

1. 任何脚本的任何部分都不会由法学硕士编写、编辑或概述。2。 视频的主题总是源自人类。3。 视频中的图像或音乐不会由人工智能生成。 如果不小心包含了某些内容，我们将尽最大努力将其删除。4。 LLM 输出作为来源不可信。

对于任何试图避免人工智能在其作品中蔓延的创作者来说，这些都是好主意。 但他们仍然提出了一个更大、更难回答的问题：生成式人工智能的结构本身就使得它很难在不减轻人类思维和判断力的情况下使用，这可能导致一种被广泛讨论的现象，即“认知投降”。 它推动我们走向各种用途——比如综合研究、集思广益、产生想法和角度——从而缩短了我们应该自己做的原始思考和发现。 那么，我们可以负责任地使用人工智能做什么呢？ 我们怎样才能设置护栏，让我们能够利用它的用处，同时又不会在这个过程中融化我们的大脑呢？

人工智能最诱人的用途恰恰是最好避免的用途

还记得 2022 年末，当 ChatGPT 首次问世时，每个人都嘲笑它蹩脚的研究能力和每一句话都会产生幻觉的倾向吗？ 我非常怀念那些日子。

许多放弃人工智能的人可能不知道，但从那时起，特别是最近几个月，大型语言模型已经变得更加智能（尤其是付费高级版本）。 它非常擅长总结利基、复杂的研究领域和辩论，并经常在没有被要求的情况下提出想法，以进行同一主题的进一步研究或写作。

这些天每当我有一个研究问题时（几乎是在我写故事的时候），我更有可能选择法学硕士而不是传统的搜索引擎。 如果我问：“为什么北美仍在砍伐老树？” 它综合了研究、新闻、观点以及其在该主题上吸收的任何其他内容：“我们正在使用本质上不可再生的生态资产来顺利过渡到可再生木材资源，”它说。 进一步探究，它会为你提出论据：“自然资源保护主义者不必证明每片古老的森林都值得保护，伐木公司应该证明砍伐具有数百年历史的林分可以满足二次生长或工程木材无法合理满足的需求。”

法学硕士旨在让认知工作变得毫不费力，但这感觉很恶心，因为它必须付出努力才有价值。

这些并不是特别聪明或有创意的想法——它们是完美的替代水平，这使得它们可以替代大多数人的想法。 人工智能可以为您在项目工作中可能遇到的每个可以想到的问题和后续行动提供简单的答案，使您无需在精神上思考问题的形状。 与人工智能概述时代之前的谷歌搜索相比，谷歌搜索虽然肯定存在问题，但至少用于将您发送到一系列来源，然后您必须自己阅读并理解这些来源。

我们大多数接触过法学硕士的人都知道这是什么感觉。 它们使用户可以轻松地了解某个主题的表面并假装理解或洞察力，并且在此过程中他们可以参与本应属于我们自己的解释性决策。 根据我的经验，即使是设计更狭窄的生成式人工智能模型也无法避免这些问题。 例如，Google 的 Gemini Notebook（以前称为 NotebookLM）允许您上传项目的所有来源（书籍、报告、论文、音频和视频记录），并根据它们包含的内容向其提问，而不是搜索整个互联网。 与通用人工智能相比，它不太容易产生彻底的错误。 我写的大多数故事都使用它——它是一个非常有用、节省时间的工具。 但它也使我能够以一种敷衍的、无上下文的方式与来源互动：人工智能可以准确地呈现我需要的部分，而不是强迫我通过阅读整个文本来形成更深层次的联系。

最好的创意作品（不仅包括艺术和写作，还包括技术和医学突破）可能来自于拥有广泛的背景关联，并能够以意想不到的方式将它们结合起来。 法国数学家亨利·庞加莱（Henri Poincaré）在他的文章《数学创造》中完美地表达了这一点，他在文中写道，繁琐、持续的有意识的努力最终会带来洞察力的闪现。

我认为这就是格林在写道人工智能可以阻止他找到“自己进入和围绕某个主题的方式”时的意思。 法学硕士旨在让认知工作变得毫不费力，但这感觉很恶心，因为它必须付出努力才有价值。 关于人工智能生成的写作，已经有人提出这样的论点：让法学硕士为你写作就失去了意义，因为写作就是思考。 但正如格林的例子所表明的那样，使用人工智能进行支持创造性过程的研究也可能是正确的。

如果您使用人工智能，请考虑制定个人人工智能政策

也许所有这些担忧都被夸大了——人类比人工智能更容易出现懒惰和逻辑不健全的思维。 这是绝对正确的，但我们自己思考的意义并不在于我们天生就擅长它。 相反，我们只有通过练习才能提高推理能力。

我不想说使用人工智能进行研究是非法的。 这是一个非常有用的工具，无法完全从桌子上取下来，而且我们不能把那个精灵放回瓶子里。 它对于识别你无法找到的最佳来源非常有帮助，但正是这些能力使其成为一把双刃剑，阻碍了更慢、更开放的探索过程。 但人工智能最大的优势——其无尽的多样性和灵活性——可以用来引导它远离最具诱惑力的用途，尤其是那些最终伤害我们的用途。

如何保持良好的人工智能卫生习惯

  • 不要使用人工智能来形成你的论文或核心论点。
  • 使用人工智能来查找而不是替换来源，并避免依赖人工智能生成的来源合成。 自己通读源材料。
  • 保持人工智能生成语言的创造性借用微观化，与使用同义词库的方式没有太大区别。
  • 留意强制使用聊天机器人。

为此，任何法学硕士用户都应该做一些非常明显的事情，比如永远不要假设人工智能的主张是准确的，并且总是阅读原始资料。 除此之外，必要的护栏取决于您自己的使用模式，但最重要的是，我认为避免训练自己期待难题的立即答案是有帮助的。

我的一位同事不会完全用它来集思广益，而是用它来为狭隘的事实问题提供来源，并在故事写完后帮助进行事实核查过程（强调“帮助”）。 综上所述，我认为在你自己起草项目之前，最好不要让人工智能对某个主题进行大量综合工作。 你做的越少，你就越不会将每个问题视为“LLM 型问题”，用格林最近的视频的话来说，你就越不会感觉自己处于大脑与人工智能融合的奇点中。

我喜欢使用人工智能的一种方式是作为增强的同义词库，找到精确的单词或短语来表达我想说的句子。 如果做得正确，我并不认为这比使用传统的同义词库更有害。我发现它可以丰富我的工作词汇。 但它必须小心谨慎地使用，对人工智能使用的短语的长度设置明确的限制——比如最多两到三个单词——并避免与该工具共享你的大部分写作内容，以免它开始建议大量重写。

当询问特定来源或大量著作的内容，或者对自己的论点进行压力测试时，如果人工智能采取苏格拉底式的方法，那么它会更好地促进我们的智力发展——推动你发现答案，而不是简单地给你一个答案。 例如，它可能会说，“第 17 页上的您的想法可能有一些相关的注意事项。 来源第 42-43 节。” 法学硕士可以在其自定义指令中指示以这种方式行事。 它还有助于简单地接触草丛——找到你需要的资源，而不是采访人工智能他们所说的内容，只需关闭聊天机器人并从头到尾阅读它们。

以对我们的大脑更健康的方式配置人工智能也会降低它的成瘾性——当你发现自己陷入与人工智能的长时间反复接触时，这通常表明出现了问题。 格林显然很难设定这个界限，他提到了不健康的“我从与法学硕士的互动中获得的多巴胺水平”。 人工智能实验室有非常强烈的商业动机，希望我们对他们的产品上瘾，除非他们自己在模型中建立不同的约束，否则很难指望普通人自己改变这些条件，因为他们对工作条款的自主权远不如格林。

尽管一些人工智能实验室的研究人员正在考虑认知萎缩的社会风​​险，但期望这些在易用性上竞争的公司在他们的模型中引入摩擦则是另一回事。 我们不应该指望这种情况很快就会发生——但我们对人工智能的影响远非无能为力。 我们可以制定自己的个人人工智能使用政策，我们可以强制执行社会规范，以防止人工智能引起的脑腐病。 就像，至少：不要把你的人工智能生成的作品发送给我。 这太粗鲁了！
